groups.title: Prisma ORM
groups.question: Explain how Prisma connects your TypeScript code to a PostgreSQL database.

followUps.Prisma Schema & Client Generation: What goes wrong if you change the Prisma schema but forget to regenerate the client?
followUps.Connection Pooling with Prisma: Why is creating a new PrismaClient on every request dangerous, especially in serverless?

evidence.text: schema.prisma defines the models, and Prisma generates a typed client from it.
If the schema changes but the client isn't regenerated, the code's types and queries don't match the real database, causing type errors or runtime failures.

notEnough: Only saying Prisma generates a client without explaining what goes wrong when it's stale.

evidence.text: Each PrismaClient has its own connection pool.
Creating a new client per request opens new pools and quickly uses up the database's connection limit.
In serverless, many short-lived instances make this worse, so you reuse one client per instance or put a pooler in front.

notEnough: Only saying reuse the client without explaining the connection limit.

groups.title: Migrations & Relations
groups.question: Walk through how you change a database schema safely and load related data efficiently with Prisma.

followUps.Prisma Migrate & Database Migrations: Why should you avoid prisma db push in production?
followUps.Relations & the N+1 Problem: What is the N+1 problem, and how would you spot and fix it in Prisma code?

evidence.text: Prisma Migrate creates migration files from schema changes, which are committed and applied in order everywhere.
db push syncs the schema directly without migration files or history, and can drop data, so it's for prototyping only.
Production uses migrate deploy to apply the committed migrations.

notEnough: Only naming the commands without explaining why db push is unsafe in production.

evidence.text: N+1 is one query for a list and then one more query for each item's related data.
It shows up as many near-identical queries in the logs, and as slowness that grows with the list size.
In Prisma you load related data together with include or select, so the database is queried a few times instead of N+1.

notEnough: Only naming the N+1 problem without explaining it or how to fix it.

groups.title: PostgreSQL Fundamentals
groups.question: Explain how PostgreSQL keeps queries fast and data correct.

followUps.Indexes & Query Planning: How would you find out why a query on a large table is slow?
followUps.Transactions & ACID Guarantees: Walk through a multi-step operation that needs a transaction, and what happens without one.

evidence.text: EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows the plan PostgreSQL used and where time was spent.
A sequential scan on a large table for a selective filter means an index is missing.
An index on the filtered or sorted columns lets the planner find rows without reading the whole table.

notEnough: Only saying add an index without explaining how to find the cause.

evidence.text: A transaction makes several statements succeed together or roll back together.
Without one, a failure halfway, like money leaving one account but not arriving in the other, leaves the data inconsistent.
Isolation keeps concurrent transactions from seeing each other's half-finished changes.

notEnough: Only spelling out what ACID stands for without explaining it.

groups.title: Data Modeling
groups.question: Explain how you design a database schema for a real production app.

followUps.Database Normalization: When would you choose to denormalize part of a schema, and what do you give up?
followUps.Soft Deletes & Audit Trails: What are the trade-offs of soft deletes compared with hard deletes?

evidence.text: Normalization stores each fact once to avoid duplicated data getting out of sync.
Denormalizing copies some data to make frequent reads faster, at the cost of keeping the copies in sync on every write.

notEnough: Only listing normal forms without explaining the trade-off.

evidence.text: A soft delete marks a row as deleted, like setting deleted_at, instead of removing it, so it can be restored and audited.
Every query must filter out deleted rows, unique constraints get harder, and the data keeps growing.
An audit trail records who changed what and when, often in a separate table.

notEnough: Only saying soft deletes keep the data without naming any downside.
